newsitem.title: USA: US rail intermodal, grain loads up from yr ago-AAR.
newsitem.headline: US rail intermodal, grain loads up from yr ago-AAR.

text.p: U.S. rail freight traffic as measured in intermodal and carloads of grain had healthy increases in the week ended November 2 over the year-ago week, the Association of American Railroads said Thursday.

AAR said that intermodal traffic, which does not include carloads, rose 7.6 percent to 178,221 trailers and containers from 165,662 in the year-ago week. Carloads of grain rose 12.2 percent to 30,398 in the week from 27,098 a year ago.
Harry Levine, AAR chief economist, called the increases "especially encouraging."
"Both (intermodal and grain) were down earlier this year, but have been showing healthy gains over last year in recent weeks," Levine said.

AAR said overall carloadings in the week rose 2.3 percent to 358,765 from 350,627 in the year-ago week. Ton-miles stood at 26.8 billion, up 2.7 percent from 26.1 billion a year ago. A ton-mile is equal to one ton of freight hauled one mile.
AAR noted that carloads of petroleum products also rose 8.6 percent in the week to 5,593 from 5,151 last year, while grain mill products increased 6.5 percent to 10,001 carloads from 9,391.

Carloads of metals and related products stood at 12,851, up 5.9 percent from 12,137 in the year-ago week. Lumber and wood products rose three percent to 5,484 carloads from 5,324 last year, while coal increased 1.9 percent to 134,977 carloads from 132,432 a year ago.
But farm products other than grain tumbled 27.4 percent to 1,840 carloads from 2,533 in the year-ago week, while motor vehicles and equipment loadings fell 2.1 percent to 20,591 from 21,042.
Pulp, paper and allied products also decreased 3.9 percent to 11,086 carloads from 11,534 a year ago, AAR said.
In the first 44 weeks of 1996, AAR said ton-miles rose two percent from the same period last year. Intermodal traffic also rose 1.4 percent, but carloads fell 0.6 percent, AAR said.

AAR also said that on a consolidated U.S.-Canadian basis for the two Canadian-based transcontinental railroads, carloads rose 8.3 percent from the year-ago week to 57,909, and intermodal increased 3.7 percent to 26,183 trailers and containers.
In the first 44 weeks of 1996, AAR said intermodal traffic for the Canadian-based railroads rose 2.1 percent from the same 1995 period, but carloads fell 1.1 percent.
